paragraphs.heading: Climate linked across distance
paragraphs.text: A teleconnection is a link between climate anomalies in places far apart, usually thousands of kilometers. The best-known example ties sea-level pressure at Tahiti to that at Darwin, Australia, and defines the Southern Oscillation. Another links air pressure over Iceland with pressure over the Azores, and is the traditional basis of the North Atlantic Oscillation, or NAO.

paragraphs.heading: Walker's discovery
paragraphs.text: The British meteorologist Sir Gilbert Walker first noticed teleconnections in the late 19th century, by calculating how records of air pressure, temperature and rainfall in different places varied together. His findings helped show that climate variability is not purely random. The name El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, itself admits that one phenomenon shapes variability in several places at once. Later, related teleconnections were found right across North America, captured in the Pacific–North American pattern.

paragraphs.heading: How the links work
paragraphs.text: In the 1980s, better observations revealed teleconnections over even larger distances. At the same time, a theory emerged that these patterns come from Rossby waves spreading out over the curved surface of the Earth. Early simple models predicted that a pattern should depend on where it was set off, but real patterns hardly depend on that at all. Newer work shows that most links from the tropics to higher latitudes can be explained surprisingly well by planetary waves moving through an atmosphere that changes with the seasons. These waves are called stationary, because the patterns persist and are partly locked in place by features such as mountain ranges.

paragraphs.heading: Forecasting far away
paragraphs.text: Teleconnections are useful for forecasting. Tropical sea surface temperatures can be predicted up to two years ahead, so knowing the patterns gives some predictability for distant places, sometimes a few seasons out. Predicting El Niño, for example, helps forecasters anticipate North American rainfall, snowfall, droughts or temperatures weeks to months in advance. In Walker's day a strong El Niño tended to go with a weaker monsoon in India, but that link weakened in the 1980s and 1990s, for reasons still argued over.

paragraphs.heading: The NAO and Europe
paragraphs.text: In Western Europe, knowing the state of the NAO helps forecasters anticipate temperature and rainfall. When it is in its positive phase in winter, westerly winds are stronger and Northern Europe gets more precipitation. In its negative phase, Northern Europe often turns dry and cold, while Southern Europe sees more storms.
